papers.title: Beyond Activation Alignment:The Alignment-Diversity Tradeoff in Task-Aware LLM Quantization
papers.abstract: Mixed-precision quantization (MPQ) has become a key technique for deploying large language models under stringent memory and compute constraints. We first identify a phenomenon that we term the Perplexity Illusion: layers ranked as important by perplexity-based sensitivity show little rank correlation with those that are most influential for complex reasoning performance, with Kendall $τ\approx 0$ in our analysis. We further reveal an Alignment-Diversity Tradeoff: using only target-task calibration data can degrade post-quantization performance, whereas incorporating general-domain data stabilizes sensitivity estimation and improves robustness across tasks. Based on these observations, we propose TASA (Task-Aware Sensitivity Analysis), a two-level framework that jointly optimizes calibration-data composition and mixed-precision bit allocation. Specifically, TASA searches for a calibration-data mixture using a training-free gradient-trace alignment criterion, and then aggregates perplexity and reasoning-oriented sensitivity signals to guide both inter-layer and intra-layer bit allocation. Experiments on LLaMA-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B reveal a precision inversion: appropriately allocated 3.5-bit models can match or surpass less task-aware 4-bit baselines. At an average precision of 3.5 bits, TASA matches or outperforms several competitive 4-bit uniform baselines in aggregate accuracy, and improves over the strongest W3 baseline on GSM8K by more than 20 absolute points on LLaMA-3-8B. These results show that calibration-data composition substantially affects task-sensitive quantization, a factor underexplored in prior work.

summary.takeaway: Calibration data composition critically influences task-aware mixed-precision quantization, enabling 3.5-bit models to match or surpass 4-bit baselines by jointly optimizing calibration data mixture and bit allocation.
summary.problem: Conventional perplexity-based sensitivity and generic calibration data fail to identify and protect reasoning-critical layers in large language models during quantization.
summary.method: TASA employs a two-level framework that optimizes calibration-data composition via gradient-trace alignment and aggregates perplexity and reasoning sensitivity signals for inter- and intra-layer mixed-precision bit allocation.
summary.evidence: Experiments on LLaMA-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B show TASA’s 3.5-bit quantized models outperform uniform 4-bit baselines and improve GSM8K accuracy by over 20 absolute points compared to the strongest W3 baseline.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis on the computational overhead of the calibration data mixture search or the generalization of TASA to tasks beyond reasoning benchmarks.
summary.why_for_you: TASA addresses the critical gap in trustworthy LLM quantization by aligning calibration data and sensitivity metrics with downstream reasoning tasks, improving robustness and efficiency.

signals.text: The Perplexity Illusion reveals near-zero Kendall τ correlation between layers ranked by perplexity sensitivity and those critical for reasoning tasks, indicating conventional PPL-based sensitivity misidentifies important layers.

TASA’s two-level mixed-precision allocation uses a training-free gradient-trace alignment criterion to optimize calibration data mixture and combines perplexity and reasoning sensitivity signals for bit allocation via integer linear programming.

Quantitative evaluation shows TASA’s 3.5-bit models match or exceed 4-bit uniform baselines in aggregate accuracy and improve GSM8K performance by more than 20 absolute points on LLaMA-3-8B, demonstrating the impact of calibration data composition.

deep_dive.overview: This work investigates the limitations of standard mixed-precision quantization (MPQ) pipelines for large language models, which rely on perplexity-based sensitivity and generic calibration data such as WikiText-2. The authors identify the Perplexity Illusion, where perplexity sensitivity rankings do not correlate with layers critical for complex reasoning tasks, undermining effective bit allocation. They further discover an Alignment-Diversity Tradeoff: exclusive use of target-task calibration data degrades quantization performance, whereas mixing general-domain data stabilizes sensitivity estimation and enhances robustness. To address these issues, the authors propose TASA, a two-level framework that first searches for an optimal calibration data mixture using a gradient-trace alignment metric without training, then aggregates perplexity and reasoning-oriented sensitivity signals to guide both inter-layer and intra-layer bit allocation via integer linear programming and group-wise salience scoring. Empirical results on LLaMA-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B demonstrate that TASA’s 3.5-bit quantized models outperform uniform 4-bit baselines and achieve substantial gains on reasoning benchmarks like GSM8K, validating the importance of calibration data composition and task-aware sensitivity integration for robust LLM quantization.

methodology.title: Calibration Data Mixture Search
methodology.detail: TASA employs a training-free gradient-trace alignment criterion to automatically optimize the composition of calibration data, balancing target-task and general-domain samples to stabilize sensitivity estimation and improve robustness.

methodology.title: Multi-Objective Sensitivity Profiling
methodology.detail: Layer-wise sensitivity is profiled using relative increases in perplexity on WikiText-2 and conditional cross-entropy losses on reasoning tasks GSM8K and ARC-Challenge, producing sensitivity vectors that capture both general and task-specific importance.

methodology.title: Inter-Layer Bit Allocation via Integer Linear Programming
methodology.detail: An integer linear programming formulation minimizes a weighted sum of perplexity and reasoning sensitivity under a global bit-budget constraint, solved efficiently by dynamic programming to produce heterogeneous per-layer bit-width assignments.

methodology.title: Intra-Layer Group-Wise Bit Allocation
methodology.detail: Within each layer, weight groups are ranked by downstream impact using GPTQ with OBS-based salience scoring, enabling fine-grained mixed-precision allocation that exploits residual sensitivity heterogeneity.

mechanism.title: Perplexity Illusion
mechanism.detail: The paper identifies that perplexity-based sensitivity rankings have near-zero Kendall τ correlation with reasoning sensitivity rankings, indicating that perplexity is an unreliable proxy for reasoning-critical layer importance in LLM quantization.

mechanism.title: Alignment-Diversity Tradeoff
mechanism.detail: Using only target-task calibration data maximizes activation alignment but reduces diversity, leading to degraded post-quantization performance; incorporating general-domain data balances alignment and diversity, stabilizing sensitivity estimation.

experiments.title: Evaluation on LLaMA-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B
experiments.detail: TASA is evaluated on large-scale LLMs with benchmarks including GSM8K and ARC-Challenge, comparing against uniform 4-bit baselines and state-of-the-art methods like W3 and TACQ, using metrics such as perplexity and conditional cross-entropy loss.

experiments.title: Baseline Implementations and Fair Comparison
experiments.detail: Baselines including GPTQ, AWQ, HQQ, and SliM-LLM are implemented with consistent group size, calibration data, and evaluation protocols to ensure fair comparison with TASA.

experiments.title: Ablation of Calibration Data Composition
experiments.detail: Experiments demonstrate that calibration solely on target-task data degrades performance, while mixed calibration data improves robustness and accuracy, validating the proposed calibration data mixture search.

findings.title: Perplexity Illusion Confirmed
findings.detail: Kendall τ correlation between perplexity sensitivity and reasoning sensitivity is approximately zero, showing that perplexity-based sensitivity fails to identify reasoning-critical layers.

findings.title: Calibration Data Composition Matters
findings.detail: Using only target-task calibration data degrades quantization quality, whereas mixing general-domain data stabilizes sensitivity estimation and improves downstream task robustness.

findings.title: TASA Outperforms Uniform Baselines
findings.detail: At an average precision of 3.5 bits, TASA matches or surpasses uniform 4-bit baselines in aggregate accuracy and improves GSM8K accuracy by over 20 absolute points on LLaMA-3-8B compared to the strongest W3 baseline.

findings.title: Intra-Layer Allocation Enhances Compression
findings.detail: Group-wise mixed-precision allocation within layers further exploits sensitivity heterogeneity, improving compression-quality tradeoffs beyond inter-layer allocation alone.

contributions: Identification of the Perplexity Illusion, revealing the disconnect between perplexity sensitivity and reasoning-critical layers in LLM quantization.
Discovery of the Alignment-Diversity Tradeoff in calibration data composition affecting task-aware quantization robustness.
Proposal of TASA, a two-level framework jointly optimizing calibration data mixture and mixed-precision bit allocation using gradient-trace alignment and multi-objective sensitivity aggregation.
Empirical demonstration that 3.5-bit TASA models outperform 4-bit uniform baselines and achieve substantial gains on reasoning benchmarks.
Integration of inter-layer integer linear programming and intra-layer group-wise allocation to exploit sensitivity heterogeneity.
limitations: The computational cost and scalability of the calibration data mixture search are not quantified or analyzed in detail.
Generalization of TASA beyond reasoning tasks and datasets such as GSM8K and ARC-Challenge is not explored.
The impact of TASA on hardware efficiency and inference latency is not reported.
Comparisons with some task-specific methods like TACQ are qualitative due to differing evaluation protocols.
open_questions: How does TASA perform on a broader range of downstream tasks beyond reasoning, such as code generation or commonsense QA?
Can the calibration data mixture search be further optimized or approximated to reduce computational overhead?
What are the implications of TASA’s bit allocation on hardware acceleration and energy efficiency in deployment?
How can the integration of task-specific gradient-based importance methods complement or improve TASA’s calibration-free approach?

papers.title: Beyond Clean Text: Evaluating Encoder and Decoder Robustness for Bangla Event Detection in Noisy Text
papers.abstract: Event detection (ED) systems are typically evaluated on clean, curated text, leaving their robustness to real-world noise largely unexplored, particularly for low-resource languages such as Bangla. We introduce a generalized Bangla news event ontology and a benchmark comprising 9,979 annotated sentences across 40 event subtypes, spanning clean news text, real-world Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) transcripts, and orthographically corrupted text. We systematically evaluate fine-tuned encoder-only models (BanglaBERT and XLM-R) alongside instruction-tuned decoder-only large language models (Llama 3 and Gemma 3). Our results reveal a clear architectural trade-off: encoder models achieve higher performance on clean text but degrade substantially under noise, whereas decoder-only LLMs are markedly more robust, particularly when event triggers are corrupted. We further show that embedding annotation guidelines during instruction tuning establishes a higher performance baseline on noisy text but yields inconsistent reductions in performance degradation across noisy conditions. Finally, model scaling consistently improves the robustness of decoder-only LLMs, while combined training on clean and noisy data serves as an effective regularization strategy that disproportionately benefits encoder architectures, significantly narrowing the robustness gap.

summary.takeaway: Decoder-only large language models exhibit superior robustness to noisy Bangla text in event detection compared to encoder-only models, especially under trigger corruption, with combined training on clean and noisy data narrowing the robustness gap.
summary.problem: Event detection systems for Bangla are predominantly evaluated on clean text, lacking robustness assessments under real-world noise such as ASR transcription errors and orthographic corruption.
summary.method: The study introduces a generalized Bangla news event ontology and benchmark dataset, systematically evaluates encoder-only (BanglaBERT, XLM-R) and decoder-only (Llama 3, Gemma 3) models under clean, ASR, and simulated orthographic noise, and explores instruction tuning with embedded annotation guidelines and combined training strategies.
summary.evidence: Empirical results show encoder models outperform on clean text but degrade significantly under noise, while decoder-only LLMs maintain higher robustness, with model scaling and combined training further improving performance, supported by statistical significance tests such as McNemar’s test.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed ablation on the impact of different noise levels on decoder-only LLMs’ robustness nor extensive analysis on the inconsistency of annotation guideline benefits across noise conditions.
summary.why_for_you: This work offers critical insights into architectural trade-offs and training strategies for robust event detection in low-resource languages, directly informing efficient adversarial training and trustworthy LLM deployment under noisy real-world conditions.

signals.text: Decoder-only LLMs like Llama 3 and Gemma 3 demonstrate markedly stronger robustness to both real-world ASR transcription noise and simulated orthographic noise compared to encoder-only models such as BanglaBERT and XLM-R, especially when event triggers are corrupted.

Instruction tuning with embedded annotation guidelines in code-format prompts establishes a higher baseline performance on noisy text but yields inconsistent reductions in performance degradation across different noisy conditions.

Combined training on clean and noisy data acts as an effective regularization strategy that disproportionately benefits encoder architectures, significantly narrowing the robustness gap between encoder-only and decoder-only models.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the underexplored problem of robustness in Bangla event detection systems under real-world noise conditions, including ASR transcription errors and orthographic corruption. The authors develop a generalized news-domain event ontology and release a benchmark dataset of 9,979 annotated sentences spanning clean news text, ASR transcripts, and synthetically corrupted text. They systematically compare encoder-only models (BanglaBERT, XLM-R) and decoder-only LLMs (Llama 3, Gemma 3) across these noisy conditions. The study formulates event detection as token classification for encoders and structured code generation for decoders, employing instruction tuning with and without embedded annotation guidelines. Results reveal a clear architectural trade-off: encoder models excel on clean text but degrade sharply under noise, whereas decoder-only LLMs maintain robustness, particularly when event triggers are corrupted. Model scaling improves decoder robustness, while combined training on clean and noisy data effectively regularizes encoders, narrowing the robustness gap. Statistical significance tests confirm these findings. This comprehensive evaluation highlights the importance of noise-aware training and model selection for robust event detection in low-resource languages.

methodology.title: Dataset Construction and Annotation
methodology.detail: The authors develop a generalized Bangla news event ontology covering 40 event subtypes and annotate 9,979 sentences from clean news text and ASR transcripts, ensuring balanced topic representation and multi-label stratified splits for training, validation, and testing.

methodology.title: Model Architectures and Formulations
methodology.detail: Encoder-only models (BanglaBERT, XLM-R) are fine-tuned for token classification to detect event triggers, while decoder-only LLMs (Llama 3, Gemma 3) are instruction-tuned to perform structured code generation representing event extraction, with prompts optionally embedding annotation guidelines as Python docstrings.

methodology.title: Noise Simulation and Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: Orthographic noise is simulated using an error generation algorithm reflecting common Bangla typographical patterns at varying word corruption rates, complemented by real-world ASR transcript noise; models are evaluated on clean, ASR, and orthographically corrupted test sets using exact trigger boundary and event type matching.

methodology.title: Instruction Tuning and Negative Sampling
methodology.detail: Decoder-only LLMs are instruction-tuned with a 1:5 positive-to-negative sampling ratio, where negative samples provide contrastive supervision to suppress hallucinated predictions; two prompting settings are compared: with and without embedded annotation guidelines.

methodology.title: Combined Training Strategy
methodology.detail: Models are trained on either clean data alone or a combined dataset of clean and noisy (ASR) data to assess the impact of joint exposure on robustness, with performance degradation measured across noise conditions.

mechanism.title: Architectural Trade-off in Robustness
mechanism.detail: Encoder-only models rely on precise token-level trigger localization, which yields high accuracy on clean text but is vulnerable to lexical corruption; decoder-only LLMs generate structured event representations conditioned on instruction prompts, enabling greater tolerance to noisy inputs and corrupted triggers. No explicit equations or causal models are provided.

experiments.title: Model Evaluation on Clean, ASR, and Orthographic Noise
experiments.detail: Encoder-only (BanglaBERT, XLM-R) and decoder-only (Llama 3, Gemma 3) models are evaluated on three test sets: Clean Test (news text), ASR Test (real-world transcripts), and Ortho Test (simulated orthographic noise at 10%-40% word corruption rates), using exact match metrics for trigger boundaries and event types.

experiments.title: Instruction Tuning Ablation
experiments.detail: Decoder-only LLMs are instruction-tuned with and without embedded annotation guidelines in prompts to assess their effect on baseline performance and robustness under noise, revealing higher baseline performance but inconsistent robustness improvements.

experiments.title: Model Scaling Impact
experiments.detail: Scaling decoder-only LLMs from 4B to 8B parameters consistently improves robustness to noisy inputs, whereas scaling encoder-only models yields limited robustness gains despite better clean-text performance.

experiments.title: Combined Training Effectiveness
experiments.detail: Training on combined clean and noisy data significantly reduces performance degradation under noise, with disproportionately larger benefits observed for encoder-only models, effectively narrowing the robustness gap with decoder-only LLMs.

findings.title: Encoder vs Decoder Performance Trade-off
findings.detail: Encoder-only models outperform decoder-only LLMs on clean Bangla news text event detection but suffer substantial performance drops under ASR and orthographic noise, while decoder-only LLMs maintain higher accuracy, especially when event triggers are corrupted.

findings.title: Instruction Tuning with Annotation Guidelines
findings.detail: Embedding detailed annotation guidelines in instruction tuning prompts raises the baseline performance of decoder-only LLMs on noisy text but does not consistently reduce performance degradation across different noise types.

findings.title: Model Scaling Benefits
findings.detail: Increasing decoder-only LLM size from 4B to 8B parameters yields consistent robustness improvements, whereas encoder-only model scaling improves clean-text accuracy but offers limited noise robustness gains.

findings.title: Combined Training as Regularization
findings.detail: Joint training on clean and noisy datasets acts as an effective regularizer, significantly mitigating noise-induced performance degradation, with encoder-only models benefiting disproportionately and narrowing the robustness gap with decoder-only LLMs.

findings.title: Statistical Significance of Robustness Differences
findings.detail: Pairwise McNemar’s exact tests at 40% word corruption rate confirm that decoder-only LLMs significantly outperform encoder-only models under trigger corruption and context corruption noise conditions.

contributions: Development of a generalized Bangla news event ontology and release of a 9,979-sentence benchmark dataset spanning clean, ASR, and orthographically corrupted text.
Systematic evaluation of encoder-only and decoder-only architectures with varying parameter sizes under multiple noisy conditions for Bangla event detection.
Application of instruction tuning with embedded annotation guidelines for structured code generation in decoder-only LLMs.
Comprehensive robustness analysis under real-world ASR noise and simulated orthographic noise, highlighting architectural trade-offs.
Demonstration that combined training on clean and noisy data effectively regularizes models and narrows robustness gaps.
limitations: Lack of detailed ablation on the impact of varying noise levels on decoder-only LLM robustness.
Inconsistent improvements from embedding annotation guidelines during instruction tuning are not fully analyzed or explained.
Limited exploration of encoder model scaling effects on robustness beyond clean-text performance.
No explicit mechanistic or causal modeling of robustness differences between architectures.
open_questions: How can instruction tuning be optimized to consistently improve robustness across diverse noisy conditions in decoder-only LLMs?
What architectural or training modifications can further enhance encoder model robustness to real-world noise in low-resource languages?
Can hybrid encoder-decoder architectures leverage the strengths of both paradigms to improve event detection robustness?
How do different types and degrees of noise interact with model scale and training strategies to affect robustness?

papers.title: Online Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: With Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training and fine-tuning shifting its focus from data volume to data quality, quality data selection has emerged as a critical research topic. Existing online data selection methods for LLM training are typically "batch-constrained", limiting optimization to local utility within random batches. To overcome this, we propose GAIA (Global Adaptive Instruction tuning via GAussian processes), a framework that formulates data valuation as a global estimation process. GAIA employs Gaussian Process regression to model continuous utility manifolds across the semantic space, utilizing an adaptive strategy fusion mechanism to dynamically prioritize high-utility samples. By casting the strategy-posterior update as an instance of the classical fixed-share Hedge framework for tracking the best expert, we inherit a dynamic-regret guarantee that characterizes GAIA's robustness under non-stationary quality scores during training. Empirical evaluations on three datasets demonstrate that GAIA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines like \greats, establishing our method as a scalable and robust solution for efficient instruction tuning.

summary.takeaway: GAIA leverages Gaussian Process regression with a fixed-share Hedge update to globally and adaptively select high-utility instruction tuning data, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines like GREATS with minimal overhead.
summary.problem: Existing online data selection methods for LLM instruction tuning are batch-constrained, limiting optimization to local utility within randomly sampled candidate pools and thus suffering from stochastic vulnerability.
summary.method: GAIA models the latent quality function over the entire training corpus using Gaussian Processes, discretizes it into strategies, and updates their posterior via a fixed-share Hedge algorithm to guide global candidate pool construction and adaptive data selection.
summary.evidence: Empirical evaluations on three instruction tuning datasets and four backbone LLMs show GAIA-GREATS achieves faster convergence and better perplexity and accuracy than baselines, adding only about 23 seconds overhead on a 13k-sample dataset.
summary.limitations: The method requires warm-up initialization with a small labeled subset and tuning of Hedge learning and mixing rates, with no explicit mechanism detailed for handling extremely large-scale datasets beyond the tested scale.
summary.why_for_you: GAIA offers a theoretically grounded, scalable, and robust framework for improving data selection quality in LLM instruction tuning, directly addressing batch-constrained limitations relevant to efficient and trustworthy LLM training.

signals.text: GAIA employs Gaussian Process regression to model a continuous latent quality function over the entire training corpus, enabling principled generalization of data valuation signals to unseen examples throughout training.
The fixed-share Hedge update mechanism maintains a posterior over discretized GP strategies, allowing dynamic adaptation to non-stationary quality scores with a provable dynamic-regret guarantee.

Empirical results on MMLU, SAMSUM, and TYDIQA datasets with LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3, Qwen, and Mistral backbones show GAIA-GREATS significantly accelerates convergence and improves test perplexity and accuracy compared to GREATS and other baselines.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the critical challenge of online data selection for instruction tuning of LLMs, where existing methods are limited by batch-constrained candidate pools sampled uniformly at random, causing local optimality and stochastic vulnerability. GAIA proposes a global data valuation framework by modeling the latent quality function over the entire training corpus using Gaussian Processes, enabling smooth generalization of utility scores to unseen data. To scale this approach, GAIA discretizes the GP into a finite set of strategies and maintains a posterior distribution over them via a fixed-share Hedge update, which adapts to the non-stationarity of quality scores as model parameters evolve. This posterior guides the sampling of candidate batches biased toward high-utility regions, which can be further refined by existing selection methods like GREATS. Empirical evaluations on multiple datasets and LLM architectures demonstrate that GAIA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with negligible computational overhead, validating its effectiveness and scalability as a robust online data selection method for instruction tuning.

methodology.title: Gaussian Process Modeling
methodology.detail: GAIA models the latent quality function over the entire training corpus as a Gaussian Process (GP) with a kernel fitted on warm-up data. This enables continuous estimation of data utility across the semantic embedding space, allowing generalization to unseen samples.

methodology.title: Strategy Discretization and Posterior Maintenance
methodology.detail: The continuous GP is discretized into a finite set of function samples called strategies. GAIA maintains a posterior distribution over these strategies using a fixed-share Hedge update with a top-k likelihood, allowing adaptation to changing data quality during training.

methodology.title: Fixed-Share Hedge Update
methodology.detail: To handle non-stationary quality scores, GAIA uses a fixed-share Hedge update that mixes the posterior with a uniform distribution at each step, preventing permanent exclusion of any strategy and providing a dynamic-regret guarantee for robustness.

methodology.title: Candidate Batch Sampling
methodology.detail: At each iteration, GAIA samples a strategy from the posterior and draws candidate batches from the training pool with probabilities proportional to the exponentiated strategy scores, controlled by a temperature parameter to balance exploitation and diversity.

methodology.title: Integration with Existing Selection Methods
methodology.detail: GAIA can be combined with methods like GREATS by first globally biasing candidate pool sampling toward high-utility regions, then applying local batch refinement to optimize quality and diversity within the batch.

mechanism.title: Dynamic Posterior Update via Fixed-Share Hedge
mechanism.detail: GAIA models the posterior over strategies with a fixed-share Hedge update that tempers each batch's evidence by a learning rate λ and mixes with a uniform distribution at rate α. This update admits a Bayesian interpretation as filtering under a Markovian switching prior, enabling recovery from shifts in the best strategy as model parameters evolve.

experiments.title: Datasets and Models
experiments.detail: Evaluations were conducted on three instruction tuning datasets: MMLU, SAMSUM, and TYDIQA, using four backbone LLMs: LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3-18B, Qwen-3.4B, and Mistral-7B.

experiments.title: Baselines and Metrics
experiments.detail: GAIA was compared against gradient-based (GradNorm), loss-prioritizing (MaxLoss, RHOLoss), semantic-aware (SBERT), and greedy optimization (GREATS) baselines, using perplexity and accuracy metrics on validation and test sets.

experiments.title: Efficiency and Overhead
experiments.detail: GAIA adds minimal computational overhead, e.g., approximately 23 seconds for GP training on a 13k-sample MMLU dataset, demonstrating practical scalability.

experiments.title: Ablations and Sensitivity
experiments.detail: The effect of sampling temperature τ and embedding dimensionality via SVD projection were analyzed, showing a trade-off between exploitation speed and batch diversity.

findings.title: Improved Convergence
findings.detail: GAIA-GREATS achieves significantly faster convergence in perplexity and accuracy on MMLU-Sociology and SAMSUM compared to all baselines, demonstrating the benefit of global adaptive data selection.

findings.title: Robustness to Non-Stationarity
findings.detail: The fixed-share Hedge update enables GAIA to adapt to evolving data quality during training, maintaining a dynamic-regret guarantee and preventing strategy collapse.

findings.title: Minimal Overhead
findings.detail: Despite the added complexity of GP modeling and posterior updates, GAIA incurs negligible runtime overhead relative to baseline training times.

findings.title: Effective Integration
findings.detail: Combining GAIA with GREATS leverages global guidance and local batch refinement, yielding superior performance over either method alone.

contributions: Formulation of data valuation as a global estimation problem using Gaussian Processes over the entire training corpus.
Introduction of a fixed-share Hedge posterior update to handle non-stationary quality scores with dynamic-regret guarantees.
A scalable and computationally efficient framework that integrates with existing online data selection methods to improve instruction tuning.
Comprehensive empirical validation on multiple datasets and LLM architectures demonstrating superior performance and efficiency.
limitations: Requires a warm-up phase with labeled data to fit the initial GP model, which may limit applicability in fully unsupervised settings.
Hyperparameters of the fixed-share Hedge update (learning rate λ and mixing rate α) require empirical tuning without automated adaptation.
Scalability beyond the tested dataset sizes and embedding dimensions is not explicitly demonstrated.
No explicit mechanism is provided for handling extremely large or streaming datasets beyond the discretized strategy approach.
open_questions: How can GAIA be extended or adapted to fully unsupervised or zero-label scenarios without warm-up initialization?
Can the fixed-share Hedge update parameters be learned or adapted online to reduce hyperparameter tuning?
What are the limits of GAIA's scalability in terms of dataset size, embedding dimensionality, and model scale?
How does GAIA perform in continual learning or streaming data scenarios where data distribution shifts significantly?

papers.title: Prototype Language Models
papers.abstract: Knowing which training examples drive outputs is fundamental to auditing, correcting, and understanding language models, yet for modern LLMs this remains expensive, approximate, and largely post-hoc. Standard language models generate tokens through a dense network pathway, causing training data's influence to be distributed across parameters rather than organized along explicit, traceable components. We introduce a prototype language model architecture, Prototypes for Interpretable Sequence Modeling (PRISM), that forms each prediction via a sparse, non-negative mixture of learned prototypes, trained with clustering objectives that anchor each prototype to coherent neighborhoods of training examples. Across architectures from 130M to 1.6B parameters trained on up to 50B tokens, prototype language models either surpass or remain within 2.5 percentage points on average downstream accuracy of matched dense baselines. We show that sparse prototype structure localizes curvature in the loss landscape, yielding a more tractable Hessian and enabling training data attribution that is ~500x faster than post hoc baselines when consuming equivalent memory. Calibrating linear prototype controllers can improve downstream accuracy by roughly 3 points while tracing those corrections back to training neighborhoods, and targeted prototype suppression can remove model behaviors without finetuning or measurable loss in generation quality.

summary.takeaway: PRISM introduces prototype-based sparse mixture modeling in language models, enabling interpretable, efficient training data attribution and controllable generation without sacrificing accuracy.
summary.problem: Standard dense language models entangle training data influence across parameters, making training data attribution computationally expensive, approximate, and post hoc.
summary.method: PRISM forms each token prediction as a sparse, non-negative mixture of learned prototypes anchored to coherent training data neighborhoods via clustering objectives.
summary.evidence: Across models from 130M to 1.6B parameters trained on up to 50B tokens, PRISM matches or slightly trails dense baselines by at most 2.5 percentage points in downstream accuracy while enabling ∼500× faster training data attribution.
summary.limitations: The paper notes limitations in sequence and document-level attribution, Hessian-aware model design, deep prototype language models, and retraining with learned attribution objectives.
summary.why_for_you: PRISM offers a scalable, interpretable architecture for LLM researchers focused on loss landscape structure, data attribution, and trustworthy model behavior control.

signals.text: PRISM’s sparse prototype structure localizes curvature in the loss landscape, yielding a more tractable Hessian that enables training data attribution approximately 500 times faster than post hoc dense parameter methods.

The method uses clustering objectives to anchor each prototype to coherent neighborhoods of training examples, forming a sparse, non-negative mixture that reconstructs next-token logits and supports interpretability and controllability.

Ablations on TinyStories show removing the prototype path causes a larger increase in cross-entropy loss than removing the residual path, indicating prototypes carry most predictive computation and improve prototype coverage and specificity.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of tracing language model outputs back to influential training data, which is difficult in standard dense transformer models due to distributed parameter influence and computationally expensive post hoc attribution methods. PRISM proposes a novel architecture where each token prediction is formed by a sparse, non-negative mixture of learned prototypes, each grounded in clusters of training examples. This design localizes curvature in the loss landscape, making the Hessian more tractable and enabling efficient, cacheable training data attribution in prototype space. Experiments across multiple model scales (130M to 1.6B parameters) and datasets (up to 50B tokens) demonstrate that PRISM matches or slightly trails dense GPT baselines in downstream accuracy while providing interpretable prototype activations. Prototype controllers further improve accuracy by about 3 points and allow tracing corrections back to training neighborhoods. Targeted suppression of prototypes can remove undesirable behaviors without finetuning or quality loss. These results establish PRISM as a scalable, interpretable, and controllable alternative to dense LMs for trustworthy language modeling.

methodology.title: Prototype Bank and Sparse Mixture
methodology.detail: PRISM maintains a prototype bank P ∈ ℝ^{d×K} where each prototype represents a cluster of training examples. At each token prediction, a sparse set of top-k prototypes is activated, and the next-token logits are formed by summing their contributions weighted by non-negative mixture coefficients, enabling interpretability and sparsity.

methodology.title: Clustering Objectives
methodology.detail: Training includes clustering regularizers (R1, R2) that encourage prototypes to anchor to coherent neighborhoods of training data, improving prototype coverage and specificity without degrading cross-entropy loss, as shown by ablations on TinyStories.

methodology.title: Cached Influence Scoring in Prototype Space
methodology.detail: Training data attribution is computed in the low-dimensional prototype space by caching sparse gradients of the prototype channel loss, enabling efficient influence function approximations that scale better than dense parameter methods.

methodology.title: Prototype Controllers
methodology.detail: Linear controllers calibrate prototype activations at inference time to improve downstream accuracy by roughly 3 points and trace corrections back to training neighborhoods, enabling controllable generation without retraining.

methodology.title: Targeted Prototype Suppression
methodology.detail: By downweighting specific prototypes associated with undesirable behaviors, PRISM can suppress those behaviors without finetuning or measurable loss in generation quality, providing a new workflow for model behavior modification.

mechanism.title: Localized Curvature in Prototype Space
mechanism.detail: PRISM’s sparse prototype structure localizes curvature in the loss landscape, making the Hessian operator H in prototype space more tractable. Influence scores SH(s→q) are computed as ∇_P L_q(P)^T H^{-1} ∇_P L_s(P), where gradients are sparse and cached, enabling efficient training data attribution.

experiments.title: Scaling and Downstream Evaluation
experiments.detail: Models from 130M to 1.6B parameters were trained on up to 50B tokens. PRISM was compared to matched dense GPT baselines on zero-shot downstream tasks including HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy/Challenge, BoolQ, and PIQA, using LM Evaluation Harness metrics.

experiments.title: TinyStories Ablations
experiments.detail: Ablations on prototype grounding (clustering strength), sparsity (top-k), and prototype bank size (K) showed that clustering improves prototype coverage and specificity with minimal CE loss, top-k controls sparsity and sharpness of active sets, and K controls granularity.

experiments.title: Training Data Attribution Efficiency
experiments.detail: Cached sparse scoring in prototype space enabled training data attribution approximately 500× faster than post hoc dense parameter methods while consuming equivalent memory, validated by influence function computations restricted to active prototypes.

findings.title: Prototype Path Dominates Predictive Computation
findings.detail: Removing the prototype path in TinyStories experiments caused a larger increase in validation cross-entropy than removing the residual path, indicating prototypes carry most of the predictive signal.

findings.title: Clustering Improves Prototype Grounding
findings.detail: Standard clustering increased prototype coverage R̄1 from 0.179 to 0.987 and improved weighted rank from 61.6 to 15.4 with negligible CE increase, demonstrating effective grounding of prototypes to training data.

findings.title: Sparse Prototype Activations Enable Interpretability
findings.detail: Top-k = 8 sparsity yielded the sharpest active prototype sets and best weighted rank (5.3), showing that sparse mixtures enhance interpretability without harming performance.

findings.title: PRISM Matches Dense Baselines in Accuracy
findings.detail: Across scales and datasets, PRISM models either surpassed or remained within 2.5 percentage points of matched dense GPT baselines on average downstream accuracy.

findings.title: Prototype Controllers Improve Accuracy and Traceability
findings.detail: Calibrating linear prototype controllers improved downstream accuracy by roughly 3 points and allowed tracing corrections back to training neighborhoods.

contributions: Introduction of PRISM, a prototype-based sparse mixture architecture for interpretable sequence modeling.
Demonstration that prototype structure localizes loss landscape curvature, enabling efficient and scalable training data attribution.
Empirical validation that PRISM matches dense GPT baselines in downstream accuracy across multiple scales and datasets.
Development of prototype controllers and targeted suppression techniques for controllable generation without finetuning.
Provision of an automated interpretability pipeline linking prototypes to coherent training data neighborhoods.
limitations: Current methods focus on token-level attribution; sequence and document-level attribution remain open challenges.
Hessian-aware model design is preliminary and requires further development for improved curvature exploitation.
Deep prototype language models beyond the tested scales are not explored, limiting understanding of scalability.
Retraining with learned attribution objectives is not addressed, leaving open how to integrate attribution into training.
open_questions: How can prototype-based attribution be extended effectively to sequence- and document-level explanations?
What architectural modifications can further improve Hessian tractability and curvature localization in prototype space?
Can prototype language models scale beyond 1.6B parameters while maintaining interpretability and efficiency?
How can learned attribution objectives be integrated into training to improve prototype grounding and model behavior?

papers.title: CausalMix: Data Mixture as Causal Inference for Language Model Training
papers.abstract: In Large Language Model (LLM) training, data mixing plays a pivotal role in determining model performance. Recent methods optimize mixture weights via proxy models, but they rely on the assumption of static data distributions. As a result, when the underlying data pool shifts, these methods require costly retraining from scratch. This limitation restricts their ability to scale seamlessly from small settings to larger data pools and model sizes. In this paper, we propose CausalMix to address this limitation by casting data mixture optimization as a causal inference problem. We formulate the statistical features of the data pool as covariates and the domain mixture as the treatment. After fitting a causal model on 512 runs of Qwen2.5-0.5B to estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE), we extrapolate the optimal mixture for an 800K data pool and apply it to train a 7B model. Furthermore, we successfully generalize the framework to long chain-of-thought data on Qwen3-4B-Base. By leveraging causal modeling to isolate confounding biases, CausalMix dynamically infers state-dependent optimal data mixtures. Extensive experiments show that the mixture guided by CausalMix consistently improves performance across multiple downstream tasks, outperforming RegMix and other baselines. In addition, we use the CATE Interpreter to provide visual analysis of the learned mixing strategy. Overall, CausalMix offers a causal and interpretable framework for optimizing LLM data mixtures.

summary.takeaway: CausalMix formulates LLM data mixture optimization as a causal inference problem, enabling dynamic, state-dependent mixture adjustments that improve downstream task performance and generalize across data scales and model sizes.
summary.problem: Existing data mixing methods for LLM training assume static data distributions and require costly retraining when data pools shift, limiting scalability and adaptability.
summary.method: CausalMix uses Double Machine Learning and causal forests to estimate Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE) of domain mixture proportions conditioned on data state covariates, enabling principled, interpretable, and transferable mixture optimization.
summary.evidence: Fitting the causal model on 512 proxy runs of Qwen2.5-0.5B and extrapolating to an 800K data pool for training a 7B model, CausalMix outperforms RegMix and other baselines across multiple downstream tasks.
summary.limitations: The causal estimator’s performance degrades with too many covariates due to limited historical meta-dataset size, and evidence on scaling covariates or proxy runs is not yet available.
summary.why_for_you: CausalMix offers a novel causal inference framework for data selection in LLM training that addresses distribution shifts and enables scalable, interpretable mixture optimization beyond static proxy models.

signals.text: CausalMix identifies state-dependent marginal data returns θ0(x) as generalized CATEs for continuous domain mixture treatments, revealing positive or negative transfer effects per domain conditioned on data state covariates.

The method employs Double Machine Learning orthogonalization and CausalForestDML with LightGBM predictors to isolate confounding effects of data state metrics such as Normalized_Loss, HES entropy, and Writing_Style.

Experiments on 512 proxy runs of Qwen2.5-0.5B with 100K-instance sub-datasets show that a three-covariate combination achieves the highest Spearman rank correlation for causal effect estimation, outperforming prior methods like RegMix.

deep_dive.overview: CausalMix addresses the challenge of optimizing data mixtures for LLM supervised fine-tuning by framing the problem as a causal inference task rather than a static hyperparameter search. It models the data pool's statistical features as covariates and the domain mixture proportions as continuous treatments, estimating the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) to capture how changes in domain proportions causally affect downstream performance under varying data states. Leveraging Double Machine Learning and causal forests, CausalMix orthogonalizes treatment and outcome variables to remove confounding biases from data quality, complexity, and difficulty metrics. This approach enables dynamic, state-dependent mixture optimization that generalizes to larger data pools and model sizes without retraining proxy models. Empirical results on Qwen2.5-0.5B proxy runs and extrapolation to a 7B model demonstrate consistent performance gains over baselines such as RegMix. The framework also provides interpretability via CATE analysis, revealing skill conflicts and data quality thresholds influencing domain effectiveness. Thus, CausalMix offers a scalable, interpretable, and principled solution for LLM data mixture optimization.

methodology.title: Causal Formulation of Data Mixture
methodology.detail: Data mixture optimization is formulated as estimating the conditional response function µ(x,z) = E[Y(t)|X=x], where X are covariates representing data state metrics and z=log(T+ε) is the log-transformed continuous treatment vector of domain mixture proportions. The model approximates µ(x,z) locally as g(x) + θ0(x)⊤z, where θ0(x) represents state-conditioned marginal data returns (generalized CATE).

methodology.title: Double Machine Learning Orthogonalization
methodology.detail: CausalMix applies Double Machine Learning to orthogonalize treatment and outcome variables with respect to covariates X, isolating the causal effect of mixture proportions on downstream performance. This reduces confounding bias from data state features such as normalized loss, entropy, and writing style.

methodology.title: Causal Model Estimation
methodology.detail: The causal model uses LightGBM as first-stage predictors for outcome and treatment models, combined with CausalForestDML as the core causal estimator. This setup captures complex interactions among covariates and treatments while controlling overfitting, achieving superior RScore compared to other regressors.

methodology.title: Policy Update and Mixture Optimization
methodology.detail: After estimating θ0(x), CausalMix performs a constrained optimization over the simplex of mixture weights using Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions to find the optimal mixture T* that maximizes expected causal performance gain, ensuring non-negativity and sum-to-one constraints.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Equations Beyond Causal Model
mechanism.detail: The paper provides a partially linear approximation µ(x,Z) ≈ g(x) + θ0(x)⊤Z for the conditional response function and derives the analytical solution for the optimal mixture policy using KKT conditions. No further mechanistic or geometric causal mechanisms are detailed.

experiments.title: Proxy Model Training and Meta-Dataset Construction
experiments.detail: 512 sub-datasets of 100K instances each are sampled from the tulu-3-sft-mixture dataset with five domain partitions. Qwen2.5-0.5B is trained on these mixtures to generate historical proxy runs (X,T,Y) for causal model fitting.

experiments.title: Covariate Selection and Evaluation
experiments.detail: Using a validation set of 64 instances, combinations of covariates from OpenDataArena metrics are evaluated by Spearman rank correlation against ground-truth scores. The best performance is achieved with three covariates: HES entropy, Normalized_Loss, and Writing_Style.

experiments.title: Causal Model Fitting and Baseline Comparison
experiments.detail: LightGBM and CausalForestDML are used to fit the causal model on the meta-dataset. The resulting CausalMix mixture policies are compared against RegMix and other baselines on downstream tasks grouped into six capabilities, showing consistent performance improvements.

experiments.title: Extrapolation to Larger Data Pools and Models
experiments.detail: The causal model trained on proxy runs is extrapolated to an 800K data pool and applied to train a 7B parameter model, demonstrating transferability and scalability without requiring new proxy experiments.

findings.title: State-Dependent Marginal Returns
findings.detail: The estimated θ0(x) reveals that increasing certain domain proportions can have positive or negative effects depending on the data state, confirming that no single static optimal mixture exists.

findings.title: Covariate Combination Importance
findings.detail: A combination of three covariates (HES entropy, Normalized_Loss, Writing_Style) yields the highest Spearman correlation for causal effect estimation, outperforming models using fewer or more covariates.

findings.title: Superior Performance Over Baselines
findings.detail: CausalMix consistently outperforms RegMix and other baselines across multiple downstream tasks and model sizes, demonstrating the effectiveness of causal mixture optimization.

findings.title: Interpretability via CATE Analysis
findings.detail: CATE analysis uncovers skill conflicts between factual knowledge and logical reasoning domains and shows how data quality thresholds influence the effectiveness of math and coding data.

contributions: Formulation of LLM data mixture optimization as a causal inference problem using continuous treatments and state-dependent covariates.
Development of a causal modeling pipeline combining Double Machine Learning, LightGBM, and CausalForestDML for estimating Conditional Average Treatment Effects.
Demonstration of scalable and transferable mixture optimization that generalizes from proxy runs to larger data pools and model sizes without retraining.
Empirical validation showing consistent performance gains over prior methods like RegMix across diverse downstream tasks.
Provision of interpretability through CATE analysis and a CATE Interpreter for visualizing learned mixing strategies.
limitations: Limited historical meta-dataset size restricts the number of covariates that can be effectively used without degrading causal estimator performance.
No direct evidence is provided on the impact of scaling proxy runs beyond 512 or incorporating additional covariates.
The approach relies on proxy models and pre-computed data metrics, which may limit applicability to domains lacking such resources.
The causal mechanism is approximated locally and partially linearly, which may not capture complex nonlinear interactions in mixture effects.
open_questions: How does increasing the number of proxy runs and covariates affect the robustness and accuracy of the causal mixture estimator?
Can the causal mixture framework be extended to incorporate nonlinear or nonparametric treatment effect models beyond partially linear approximations?
What are the limits of transferability when extrapolating causal mixture policies to substantially different data pools or model architectures?
How can the framework be adapted or integrated with online or continual learning settings where data distributions evolve dynamically?

papers.title: Can Agents Generalize to the Open World? Unveiling the Fragility of Static Training in Tool Use
papers.abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents demonstrate proficiency in static benchmarks, their deployment in real-world scenarios is hindered by the dynamic nature of user queries, tool sets, and interaction dynamics. To address this generalization gap, we formalize OpenAgent (Tool-Use Agent in Open-World), a problem setting characterized by distributional shifts across query, action, observation, and domain dimensions. To systematically diagnose its impact, we construct a controlled sandbox environment where we define fine-grained environmental shifts across a four-tier hierarchy, Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization, and conduct a comprehensive series of experiments. Our analysis yields a series of key insights, demonstrating that agents trained via both Supervised Fine-Tuning(SFT) and Reinforcement Learning suffer from varying degrees of performance degradation when confronting open environmental shifts. Building on these insights, we propose Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning, a disturbance-based intervention strategy for SFT that lays the foundation for enhancing agent robustness and utility in realistic environments. Our code will be released at: https://github. com/LAMDA-NeSy/OpenAgent.

summary.takeaway: LLM agents trained via Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning exhibit significant performance degradation under open-world distributional shifts, which can be partially mitigated by Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning.
summary.problem: Current LLM agents trained under static assumptions fail to generalize effectively to dynamic, open-world tool-use environments characterized by shifts in queries, tools, interactions, and domains.
summary.method: The authors formalize the OpenAgent problem setting, construct a controlled sandbox environment with a four-tier hierarchy of environmental shifts, and propose Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning to improve robustness.
summary.evidence: Comprehensive experiments in the sandbox environment demonstrate that both SFT and RL agents suffer from distinct failure modes and performance drops under open-world shifts, with PAFT improving SFT robustness.
summary.limitations: The study focuses on a synthetic sandbox environment and does not provide evidence of PAFT’s effectiveness in fully real-world, large-scale deployments or across diverse tool-use domains.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a rigorous framework and empirical insights into the generalization challenges of tool-using LLM agents, offering a novel fine-tuning strategy relevant for enhancing trustworthy and efficient adversarial training.

signals.text: The study identifies symbolic anchoring as a critical failure mode in Supervised Fine-Tuning agents, causing brittle reliance on shallow patterns that degrade performance under tool schema shifts.

Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning (PAFT) injects controlled observation anomalies and symbolic noise during training to decouple models from memorization and enhance robustness to open-world perturbations.

Experimental results show that Reinforcement Learning agents maintain higher active exploration scores (>0.86 AES) under tool redirection and value redirection shifts, whereas SFT agents’ scores collapse near zero.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the critical gap in generalization of LLM agents trained under static assumptions when deployed in dynamic, open-world environments. The authors formalize the OpenAgent setting, capturing distributional shifts across user queries, tool sets, interaction dynamics, and task domains. To systematically analyze these shifts, they design a controlled sandbox environment with a four-tier hierarchy—Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization—allowing precise injection of perturbations. Through extensive experiments comparing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents, the study reveals distinct failure modes: SFT agents suffer from symbolic anchoring and trajectory overfitting, while RL agents exhibit boundary blindness due to reward structure biases. To mitigate these issues, the authors propose Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning (PAFT), a data-centric approach that introduces controlled noise during training to improve robustness. Empirical evidence demonstrates PAFT’s effectiveness in restoring generalization capabilities, highlighting the fragility of static training and the necessity of disturbance-based interventions for real-world tool-use agent deployment.

methodology.title: OpenAgent Formalization
methodology.detail: The agent is modeled as a sequential decision-making process M = ⟨Q, A, O, π⟩, where Q is user queries, A is tool action space, O is observation space, and π is the policy. The OpenAgent setting characterizes distributional shifts across queries (∆Q), actions (∆A), observations (∆O), and domains (∆D), focusing on generalization when test distributions diverge from training.

methodology.title: Controlled Sandbox Environment
methodology.detail: A synthetic sandbox environment is constructed to isolate and systematically inject environmental shifts across four tiers: Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization. This controlled setup avoids transient noise from real-world APIs, enabling precise evaluation of agent robustness to open-world perturbations.

methodology.title: Training Paradigms and Baselines
methodology.detail: The study compares full-parameter Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Reinforcement Learning (RL) with the GRPO framework. Both models are trained to convergence under comparable computational budgets in the closed environment to establish baselines.

methodology.title: Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning (PAFT)
methodology.detail: PAFT is a disturbance-based intervention for SFT that injects controlled observation anomalies and symbolic noise into training trajectories. This approach aims to prevent shallow pattern memorization and improve generalization by forcing the model to learn robust representations under noisy conditions.

mechanism.title: Failure Modes in Training Paradigms
mechanism.detail: SFT agents exhibit symbolic anchoring, where they overfit to specific tool invocation patterns, leading to brittle performance under schema shifts. RL agents, while better at semantic grounding, suffer from boundary blindness caused by teleological biases in reward structures, limiting their adaptability to novel tool configurations.

experiments.title: Evaluation of Instruction Robustness (∆Q)
experiments.detail: Agents are tested on their ability to handle instruction blurring and information redundancy, simulating real-world user input variability. The evaluation uses a dataset of 6,050 training and 880 evaluation samples with strict separation to prevent pattern leakage.

experiments.title: Tiered Environmental Shift Experiments
experiments.detail: Experiments inject perturbations across Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization tiers in the sandbox. Metrics include task success rates and Active Exploration Scores (AES) to quantify agent adaptability under null returns, error returns, tool redirection, and value redirection.

experiments.title: Comparison of SFT and RL Agents
experiments.detail: Both paradigms are trained on the same backbone and evaluated under identical conditions. RL agents maintain near-perfect AES (>0.86) under tool redirection shifts, whereas SFT agents’ AES collapse near zero, indicating distinct robustness profiles.

experiments.title: PAFT Intervention Evaluation
experiments.detail: PAFT is applied to SFT agents by augmenting training data with controlled noise. Results show improved robustness and utility in open environments, partially restoring generalization lost due to symbolic anchoring.

findings.title: Performance Degradation under Open-World Shifts
findings.detail: Both SFT and RL agents experience significant performance drops when exposed to distributional shifts in queries, tools, interactions, and domains, confirming the fragility of static training assumptions.

findings.title: Distinct Failure Modes for SFT and RL
findings.detail: SFT agents suffer from trajectory overfitting and symbolic anchoring, leading to brittle tool invocation, while RL agents show boundary blindness due to reward teleology, limiting their semantic adaptability.

findings.title: RL Agents’ Superior Active Exploration
findings.detail: Under tool redirection and value redirection perturbations, RL agents maintain high Active Exploration Scores (>0.86), indicating better adaptability compared to SFT agents whose scores collapse near zero.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning
findings.detail: PAFT improves SFT agents’ robustness by injecting controlled noise during training, mitigating symbolic anchoring and enhancing generalization to open-world shifts.

contributions: Formalization of the OpenAgent problem setting capturing multi-dimensional distributional shifts in tool-use environments.
Development of a controlled sandbox environment with a four-tier hierarchy for systematic evaluation of agent robustness.
Identification of critical failure modes: symbolic anchoring in SFT and boundary blindness in RL.
Proposal of Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning (PAFT) as a data-centric method to enhance SFT robustness.
Comprehensive empirical analysis comparing SFT and RL paradigms under open-world perturbations.
limitations: Evaluation is limited to a synthetic sandbox environment, which may not fully capture complexities of real-world tool-use scenarios.
PAFT’s effectiveness is demonstrated only on SFT agents and not extended to RL or hybrid paradigms.
The study does not explore scalability of PAFT to larger models or diverse tool sets beyond the tested tasks.
No direct evidence is provided on long-term deployment stability or user-centric metrics in open environments.
open_questions: How can PAFT or similar disturbance-based methods be integrated with RL or hybrid training paradigms to improve robustness?
What are the scalability limits of PAFT when applied to larger LLMs and more complex, heterogeneous tool ecosystems?
Can the four-tier hierarchy of environmental shifts be extended or refined to better model real-world deployment dynamics?
How do these findings translate to real-world APIs and user interactions with noisy, evolving tool sets?
